fomalhaut.name: Fomalhaut
fomalhaut.introduction: is a nearby triple system whose brilliant white primary marks the mouth of the Southern Fish. Its much fainter companions, the orange dwarf TW Piscis Austrini and red dwarf LP 876-10, are spread across an exceptionally wide region of space.

sections.title: Belts beyond the star
sections.text: Webb revealed nested belts of dusty debris around Fomalhaut A. Collisions between smaller bodies continually replenish the dust, making this a nearby laboratory for studying how planetary systems evolve.

source.title: NASA: Webb reveals Fomalhaut’s debris belts

sections.title: A planet that became a dust cloud
sections.text: The object announced as Fomalhaut b is now interpreted as expanding collision debris. In 2025, astronomers reported a second newly appearing cloud in Hubble images: a rare opportunity to watch destructive collisions around another star.

source.title: NASA: Hubble observes new collision debris around Fomalhaut, 2025

cns5-4607.name: Vega
cns5-4607.introduction: is the brilliant blue-white star in Lyra and a corner of the Summer Triangle. Its long role as a reference for stellar brightness helped make it one of astronomy’s most closely studied stars.

sections.title: A fast spinner seen pole-on
sections.text: Vega rotates rapidly, but we look almost along its spin axis. Its equator bulges outward and is cooler than its poles, so its apparently simple point of light hides a strongly uneven surface.

sections.title: A remarkably smooth debris disk
sections.text: Hubble and Webb observations published in 2024 showed a broad, unusually smooth disk of dust. They found no obvious imprint of large planets sculpting it; a debris disk alone is not proof of a detected planet.

source.title: NASA: Hubble and Webb probe Vega’s smooth disk, 2024

cns5-1912.name: Pollux
cns5-1912.introduction: is an orange giant in Gemini, brighter than its apparent twin Castor. The two are unrelated systems: Pollux is an evolved star, while Castor is a family of six stars.

sections.title: A giant with a giant planet
sections.text: Pollux b, also named Thestias, was established through the star’s rhythmic Doppler wobble in 2006. It takes about 590 days to orbit and has a minimum mass more than twice Jupiter’s.

sections.title: A preview of stellar aging
sections.text: Pollux has expanded after exhausting the hydrogen in its core. Its cool orange surface and enlarged size show how a familiar-looking star can be in a very different phase of life from the Sun.

bright-denebola.name: Denebola
bright-denebola.introduction: is a white star marking the tail of Leo, about 36 light-years away. Its name preserves that position in the lion’s figure.

sections.title: Dust from a debris system
sections.text: Denebola emits more infrared light than its stellar surface can explain. Cool circumstellar dust produces the excess, pointing to debris left by collisions among smaller orbiting bodies.

sections.title: A spinning, pulsating star
sections.text: It rotates rapidly and shows small Delta Scuti pulsations. These slight changes in brightness let astronomers investigate a stellar interior that cannot be seen directly.

cns5-3517.name: Arcturus
cns5-3517.introduction: is the orange beacon in Boötes and the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere. Following the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle leads the eye toward it.

sections.title: A Sun-like mass, a giant envelope
sections.text: Models place its mass close to the Sun’s, while its radius has expanded to roughly 25 times the Sun’s. It has exhausted its central hydrogen and shines as a red giant, with a cooler surface spread over a much larger area.

sections.title: An older Galactic traveler
sections.text: Its relatively low iron abundance and motion identify it with an older stellar population. Its conspicuous movement against distant stars was among the early evidence that the supposedly fixed stars move through space.

cns5-3442.name: Muphrid
cns5-3442.introduction: is the yellow-white star near Arcturus in Boötes. The two are also neighbors in three dimensions, separated by only a few light-years, rather than merely lining up in our sky.

sections.title: Caught between dwarf and giant
sections.text: Muphrid is a subgiant, expanding as it leaves its long period of core hydrogen burning. Measurements of its size and oscillations help test models of this relatively brief transition.

sections.title: A companion remains uncertain
sections.text: A roughly 494-day spectroscopic orbit has been reported, but attempts to resolve the proposed companion have not confirmed it. The visible star is much better characterized than its possible partner.

capella.name: Capella
capella.introduction: is the golden light in Auriga, usually seen as one star but actually a family of four. Two luminous giants dominate the view; a distant pair of red dwarfs completes the system.

sections.title: Two giants in one orbit
sections.text: The bright pair circles every 104 days. They formed together with similar masses, yet differ in temperature and evolutionary state, making their measured masses and sizes a valuable test of stellar evolution.

sections.title: Small stars far from the spotlight
sections.text: Capella H and L are faint red dwarfs far from the giants. Their presence illustrates how one naked-eye star can contain both enormous evolved stars and inconspicuous, long-lived companions.

orb6-17349+1234-a-b.name: Rasalhague
orb6-17349+1234-a-b.introduction: is a binary at the head of Ophiuchus. A bright white primary and a much fainter, cooler dwarf orbit one another in about 8.6 years.

sections.title: A star pulled out of round
sections.text: The primary spins so rapidly that it bulges at the equator. Its poles are hotter and brighter than its equatorial regions, an effect called gravity darkening.

sections.title: Weighing a distorted star
sections.text: Observations of the companion’s orbit provide a dynamical mass for the primary. That independent measurement helps astronomers test models of rapid rotation, which complicates the usual interpretation of stellar temperature and brightness.

bright-alderamin.name: Alderamin
bright-alderamin.introduction: is the brightest star in Cepheus, the northern king. This nearby white star looks steady to the eye, but its surface is far from uniform.

sections.title: A day shorter than ours
sections.text: Alderamin turns in less than half an Earth day. Interferometers have measured its flattened shape and the temperature contrast between hotter poles and a cooler equator.

sections.title: Listening to the star
sections.text: Tiny brightness oscillations include more than one family of pulsations. Together with its directly measured shape, these offer complementary clues to how a rapidly rotating star behaves inside.

msc-07346+3153.name: Castor
msc-07346+3153.introduction: is the white member of Gemini’s famous pair of “twins.” Unlike the orange giant Pollux, Castor is a six-star system arranged as three close binaries.

sections.title: Pairs within a family
sections.text: A telescope separates the bright A and B components, but spectroscopy reveals that each has a close companion. The more distant Castor C is another close pair, made of red dwarfs.

sections.title: Eclipses and flares
sections.text: Castor Ca and Cb are the red-dwarf pair YY Geminorum. They eclipse one another every 0.814 days. Spectroscopy combined with the eclipsing inclination gives each a mass close to 0.606 Suns; their measured sizes also help test models of magnetically active small stars.

source.title: Kochukhov & Shulyak 2019: the YY Gem eclipsing pair
Torres et al. 2022: Castor orbits and dynamical masses

bright-caph.name: Caph
bright-caph.introduction: is the star at one end of Cassiopeia’s W. It is a yellow-white star evolving toward the giant phase.

sections.title: A pulse every few hours
sections.text: Caph is a Delta Scuti variable. It brightens and fades slightly over roughly 2.5 hours as the star pulsates; the changes are too subtle to stand out in casual naked-eye viewing.

sections.title: A flattened surface
sections.text: Rapid rotation gives Caph an oblate shape and makes its poles hotter than its equator. Combining its pulsations with interferometric measurements lets astronomers examine both its interior and its surface.

bright-zosma.name: Zosma
bright-zosma.introduction: is a white star on the back of Leo. It is hotter and larger than the Sun, but still belongs to the long-lived, hydrogen-burning main sequence.

sections.title: A shape measured with light
sections.text: Interferometry measures its apparent diameter by combining light collected at separated telescopes. Rapid rotation makes Zosma oblate, so a single spherical radius only approximates its shape.

sections.title: From white star to giant
sections.text: Its present appearance represents an earlier evolutionary stage than nearby-looking orange giants. As its central hydrogen runs out, it will expand and cool, changing both its size and its color.

orb6-01546+2049-a-b.name: Sheratan
orb6-01546+2049-a-b.introduction: is a close binary marking one of the ram’s horns in Aries. A white primary dominates the light, concealing a fainter companion broadly similar in spectral type to the Sun.

sections.title: An elongated orbit
sections.text: The pair follows a strongly eccentric orbit lasting about 107 days. Their separation changes considerably during each circuit, unlike the nearly circular paths of most major planets in our Solar System.

sections.title: A binary revealed by two methods
sections.text: Doppler shifts reveal the orbital motion, while interferometry separates the light of the components. Combining the two methods turns an unresolved-looking star into a system with measurable stellar masses.

bright-menkent.name: Menkent
bright-menkent.introduction: is an orange giant in Centaurus. It lies farther north in the constellation than Alpha and Beta Centauri, bringing part of the Centaur into view for many northern observers.

sections.title: Helium in the core
sections.text: Menkent is generally interpreted as a red-clump giant, generating energy by fusing helium in its core. That places it beyond the first expansion that follows the exhaustion of central hydrogen.

sections.title: A southern counterpart to Pollux
sections.text: Its color and evolutionary state resemble those of Pollux in Gemini. Stars with such similar spectra help astronomers compare giant-star atmospheres without relying on one object alone.

bright-epsilon-scorpii.name: Epsilon Scorpii
bright-epsilon-scorpii.introduction: is the orange giant also named Larawag, partway along the curved body of Scorpius. A faint red-dwarf companion shares its motion; the pair is much closer to us than many of the constellation’s hot blue stars.

sections.title: A giant’s subtle heartbeat
sections.text: Small, Sun-like oscillations have been measured in its light. These are excited by convection and reveal information about the interior of a star whose surface has expanded far beyond the Sun’s.

sections.title: A name from Australia
sections.text: Larawag comes from the Wardaman people of northern Australia. Its adoption into the international star-name catalog recognizes a sky tradition distinct from the Greek scorpion figure.

bright-hamal.name: Hamal
bright-hamal.introduction: is the orange giant that marks the head of Aries. Its light comes from an enlarged, cooler star rather than a Sun-like dwarf.

sections.title: A planet around an aging star
sections.text: A giant planet was reported in 2011 from Doppler measurements. Its orbit lasts about 381 days, showing that planetary systems can remain observable after their host has begun its giant-star evolution.

sections.title: Where spring once began
sections.text: Aries once contained the Sun at the March equinox. Earth’s slowly changing axis has shifted that point into Pisces, but the historical connection survives in the term “First Point of Aries.”

bright-aldebaran.name: Aldebaran
bright-aldebaran.introduction: is the orange eye of Taurus. It appears embedded in the V-shaped Hyades, but lies in the foreground and is not a member of that star cluster.

sections.title: A swollen, aging star
sections.text: Aldebaran has used up its central hydrogen and expanded to tens of solar radii. Its large apparent diameter makes it an important target for measurements of giant-star surfaces and atmospheres.

sections.title: A disputed planet signal
sections.text: Long-period changes in its radial velocity have been interpreted as a giant planet, but stellar variability complicates the signal. The proposed planet remains disputed rather than a secure explanation for every measured wobble.

bright-unukalhai.name: Unukalhai
bright-unukalhai.introduction: is the brightest star in Serpens, in the separate head portion of the divided constellation. Its traditional name refers to the serpent’s neck.

sections.title: An orange giant with a spectral clue
sections.text: Its spectrum contains unusually strong cyanogen absorption bands. These molecular signatures are clues to atmospheric composition, rather than a change that can be recognized from the star’s naked-eye color.

sections.title: Beyond central hydrogen burning
sections.text: Unukalhai is an evolved giant, probably burning helium in its core. Its cool outer layers have expanded, allowing it to radiate far more light than the Sun despite a lower surface temperature.

msc-20462+3358.name: Aljanah
msc-20462+3358.introduction: is the orange giant marking one wing of Cygnus. It is also known by the older name Gienah, which has been used for a different star in Corvus.

sections.title: A giant with an unseen partner
sections.text: Long-term spectroscopy reveals a companion in a highly eccentric orbit lasting roughly 53 years. The orbit is detected through the bright giant’s changing line-of-sight velocity.

sections.title: An ancient wing star
sections.text: The primary is an old, evolved star with a mass fairly close to the Sun’s. Its bright appearance comes from an expanded giant envelope, contrasting with the young, massive supergiants elsewhere in Cygnus.

bright-alphecca.name: Alphecca
bright-alphecca.introduction: is the brightest jewel in the arc of Corona Borealis, the Northern Crown. It is a close binary whose white primary outshines a cooler companion.

sections.title: A crown jewel that dims
sections.text: The stars orbit every 17.4 days and pass in front of one another from our viewpoint. The resulting eclipses are shallow enough to escape casual naked-eye notice.

sections.title: A lively smaller companion
sections.text: The cooler star has a magnetically active, X-ray-emitting corona. Eclipses and orbital velocities together help separate the properties of two stars that otherwise appear as a single point.

msc-10084+1158.name: Regulus
msc-10084+1158.introduction: is the blue-white heart of Leo and a multiple system close to the ecliptic. The bright star’s close companion and a wider pair make its simple naked-eye appearance deceptive.

sections.title: An almost breakneck spin
sections.text: Regulus rotates in about 16 hours, giving it a bulging equator and hotter poles. It is a striking example of how fast rotation changes both a star’s shape and its apparent temperature.

sections.title: A stripped companion
sections.text: A very faint, low-mass stellar companion orbits in about 40 days. Spectroscopy supports a stripped, pre-white-dwarf identity: past mass transfer likely helped spin up the bright primary. A much wider pair adds another layer to the system.

source.title: Gies et al. 2020: Spectroscopic detection of Regulus’s pre-white-dwarf companion

msc-13239+5456.name: Mizar
msc-13239+5456.introduction: is the famous double star in the Big Dipper’s handle, near the fainter Alcor. Mizar itself contains four stars, arranged as two close binaries.

sections.title: A double that became a quadruple
sections.text: A small telescope resolves Mizar A and B. Spectroscopy then reveals that each visible component has its own close companion: two nested levels of multiplicity in a familiar sky landmark.

sections.title: A history of hidden stars
sections.text: Mizar A became the first spectroscopic binary to be recognized. Its doubled spectral lines demonstrated that starlight can reveal companions too close together for a telescope to separate directly.

orb6-05595+4457-aa-ab.name: Menkalinan
orb6-05595+4457-aa-ab.introduction: is a bright binary in Auriga made of two very similar white stars. Both are larger and hotter than the Sun.

sections.title: Nearly matching stars, grazing eclipses
sections.text: The pair circles in about 3.96 days and undergoes shallow eclipses. A 2026 analysis combined resolved CHARA observations with spectra and light curves, measuring masses of about 2.36 and 2.29 Suns and radii of about 2.75 and 2.62 Suns.

sections.title: Unusual metal lines
sections.text: Both stars show metallic-line spectra, with some chemical elements unusually prominent. Such abundance patterns form in stellar atmospheres; they do not mean the entire stars have the same exaggerated composition.

source.title: Jonak et al. 2026: the joint beta Aurigae solution

bright-ankaa.name: Ankaa
bright-ankaa.introduction: is the orange beacon in Phoenix, the southern firebird. Its visible light is dominated by an evolved giant.

sections.title: A slow spectroscopic orbit
sections.text: Ankaa is a binary with an orbital period of about 10.5 years. The companion is revealed through the motion of the bright star, even though the system looks like one point to the eye.

sections.title: The firebird’s name
sections.text: Ankaa comes from the Arabic name for the phoenix. The star links a traditional name to one of the southern constellations introduced into European astronomy during the age of ocean exploration.

bright-alioth.name: Alioth
bright-alioth.introduction: is the brightest star in Ursa Major, partway along the Big Dipper’s handle. It belongs to the moving group shared by several of the Dipper’s central stars.

sections.title: Chemical patches on a magnetic star
sections.text: Alioth has an unusual spectrum and a magnetic field. Uneven surface abundances rotate in and out of view, changing the appearance of its light over about five days.

sections.title: A wobble with another explanation
sections.text: That repeating variation once inspired a proposed substellar companion. Rotation and chemical structure provide the accepted explanation for the five-day pattern; it should not be presented as an established planet.

bright-phecda.name: Phecda
bright-phecda.introduction: is one of the bowl stars of the Big Dipper. It travels with the Ursa Major moving group, a family of stars sharing a common origin.

sections.title: A hidden partner in the motion
sections.text: An astrometric wobble reveals a cooler companion on a roughly 20-year orbit. Tracking a star’s changing position can expose a partner even when its light is difficult to isolate.

sections.title: A hot star with emission
sections.text: The bright component is an A-type star whose spectrum includes emission. Its blue-white appearance contrasts with the much cooler companion, showing how one catalog point can combine very different stars.

bright-merak.name: Merak
bright-merak.introduction: is the lower of the Big Dipper’s two familiar pointer stars. Extending the line from Merak through Dubhe leads toward Polaris.

sections.title: A member of a moving family
sections.text: Merak belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, along with several other central Dipper stars. Their similar motions reflect a shared history, although the whole seven-star pattern is not one bound system.

sections.title: Dust beyond the star
sections.text: An excess of infrared radiation indicates a circumstellar debris disk. The dust offers evidence of orbiting material around this white star, without itself establishing the presence of a detected planet.

orb6-19026-2953-a-b.name: Ascella
orb6-19026-2953-a-b.introduction: is a triple system at the lower corner of Sagittarius’s Teapot handle. Its blended white light hides two different scales of orbital motion.

sections.title: An orbit measured across decades
sections.text: The visual pair completes an orbit in about 21 years. Repeated measurements of their separation and orientation trace their motion around a shared center of mass.

sections.title: A closer pair inside the pair
sections.text: A companion reported in 2023 turns one component into a much closer binary, with an estimated orbit of about a month. A nearby star long listed as a distant companion is instead an unrelated background object.

source.title: Waisberg et al. 2023: Discovery of a close companion to Ascella A

orb6-17104-1544-a-b.name: Sabik
orb6-17104-1544-a-b.introduction: is a binary in Ophiuchus whose two white stars are similar in brightness. To the unaided eye, their light merges into one of the constellation’s brightest points.

sections.title: A highly eccentric partnership
sections.text: The stars take roughly 88 years to complete a strongly elongated orbit. Their changing separation provides a long-term example of orbital motion on a timescale comparable to a human lifetime.

sections.title: A useful stellar comparison
sections.text: Because the two stars formed together and have similar spectral types, they offer a controlled comparison of stellar properties. Their combined light must still be distinguished from the properties of either individual component.

bright-gacrux.name: Gacrux
bright-gacrux.introduction: is the reddish star at the top of the Southern Cross. It is a comparatively nearby giant, in contrast to the more distant hot stars that define much of Crux.

sections.title: A red star in a blue cross
sections.text: Its cool surface produces the orange-red color visible beside the Cross’s blue-white stars. Expansion makes the giant luminous despite that lower surface temperature.

sections.title: A gently changing atmosphere
sections.text: Gacrux varies semi-regularly and loses material into its surroundings. Its slow changes and extended atmosphere help astronomers study how evolved stars return gas to interstellar space.

msc-03082+4057.name: Algol
msc-03082+4057.introduction: is the “Demon Star” in Perseus, a multiple system famous for predictable fades. Its bright appearance is dominated by a close eclipsing pair with a third star farther out.

sections.title: An eclipse you can follow
sections.text: About every 2.87 days, the cooler star crosses the hotter star and the system dims noticeably. Comparing Algol with nearby stars over several hours reveals orbital geometry without needing a telescope.

sections.title: The Algol paradox
sections.text: The less massive member is the more evolved one. It was originally more massive, aged faster, and then transferred gas to its partner, reversing the masses and revealing how binary interaction can rewrite a star’s history.

bright-diphda.name: Diphda
bright-diphda.introduction: is the brightest star in Cetus, also called Deneb Kaitos. Its orange light comes from a giant that has moved beyond core hydrogen burning.

sections.title: A hot atmosphere above a cool surface
sections.text: X-ray observations reveal energetic plasma around the star. Its outer atmosphere can reach temperatures of millions of degrees even though the visible photosphere is cooler than the Sun’s.

sections.title: Giant-star magnetic activity
sections.text: Long-lasting episodes of enhanced high-energy emission distinguish Diphda from a quietly glowing ball. It helps astronomers investigate how magnetic activity survives or changes as a star expands into a giant.

msc-00084+2905.name: Alpheratz
msc-00084+2905.introduction: is the brightest star in Andromeda and a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. The apparent overlap of those sky figures has given it a history in both constellations.

sections.title: A binary behind the square
sections.text: A hot primary and a fainter companion orbit in about 97 days. Their blended light makes one bright landmark, while spectroscopy separates their orbital motion.

sections.title: Mercury and manganese in the light
sections.text: The primary has unusually strong signatures of heavy elements, including mercury and manganese. Selective movement of elements through its atmosphere produces chemical patches and abundances very different from the Sun’s.

bright-alnair.name: Alnair
bright-alnair.introduction: is the brightest star in Grus, the Crane. It is a hot blue-white star, much more massive and luminous than the Sun.

sections.title: A rapid rotator
sections.text: Its broadened spectral lines show that the surface is spinning quickly. Rotation complicates the interpretation of a star’s spectrum, since different parts of the visible surface move toward or away from us.

sections.title: A southern navigation light
sections.text: Alnair is one of the bright stars used in celestial navigation. Its prominent position in the southern sky makes it useful even though it is unfamiliar to observers at high northern latitudes.

bright-ruchbah.name: Ruchbah
bright-ruchbah.introduction: is one of the five stars that draw Cassiopeia’s W. Its white light comes from a star larger and hotter than the Sun.

sections.title: An eclipse claim with uncertainty
sections.text: Older reports described small eclipses on a roughly 759-day cycle. Modern observations have not consistently reproduced them, so the proposed eclipsing behavior remains uncertain.

sections.title: The queen’s knee
sections.text: The traditional name refers to a knee in the imagined figure of Cassiopeia. It is a reminder that the familiar W is only a compact part of the much larger constellation figure.

bright-alkaid.name: Alkaid
bright-alkaid.introduction: is the blue-white star at the end of the Big Dipper’s handle. It is one of the hottest bright members of the familiar pattern.

sections.title: A different journey
sections.text: Unlike the five central Dipper stars, Alkaid is not a member of the Ursa Major moving group. The recognizable shape therefore combines stars with different origins and paths through the Galaxy.

sections.title: A spectral yardstick
sections.text: Its spectrum has long served as a reference for classifying hot B-type stars. These standard stars give astronomers stable comparison points when identifying the temperatures and luminosity classes of less familiar objects.

orb6-06377+1624-aa-ab.name: Alhena
orb6-06377+1624-aa-ab.introduction: is the white star marking a foot of Gemini. Its light is dominated by a hot primary, but it is a binary rather than a solitary star.

sections.title: A long, eccentric orbit
sections.text: The companion completes an orbit in roughly 12.6 years. Its strongly changing separation is traced by combining spectroscopy with measurements that resolve the pair.

sections.title: Unequal stars formed together
sections.text: The bright primary has begun to expand beyond its main-sequence state, while its less massive companion remains a hydrogen-burning star. Their shared origin makes the pair useful for comparing how stars of different masses evolve.

orb6-10468-4925-a-b.name: Mu Velorum
orb6-10468-4925-a-b.introduction: is a southern binary with a yellow giant and a fainter, less evolved companion. Their orbit takes more than a century.

sections.title: A giant flare
sections.text: In 1998, the Extreme Ultraviolet Explorer observed an exceptionally powerful high-energy flare. It showed that an evolved giant can still sustain dramatic magnetic activity above its comparatively cool visible surface.

sections.title: Two stages in one system
sections.text: The bright star has expanded into a giant, while its companion remains on the main sequence. Their shared origin makes the pair useful for comparing how stars with different masses age.

bright-miaplacidus.name: Miaplacidus
bright-miaplacidus.introduction: is a white star in Carina and one of the brightest lights in the southern sky. Its far-southern position keeps it below the horizon for many northern observers.

sections.title: A giant that still spins quickly
sections.text: Although it has expanded beyond its earlier main-sequence size, Miaplacidus retains rapid rotation. Broad spectral lines reveal the motion of its surface.

sections.title: Part of the old ship
sections.text: Carina represents the keel of the ancient, much larger constellation Argo Navis. Miaplacidus is one of the bright stars that remain as landmarks after the ship was divided into separate modern constellations.

msc-11037+6145.name: Dubhe
msc-11037+6145.introduction: is the orange star at the outer edge of the Big Dipper’s bowl. Together with Merak it forms the pointer pair used to find Polaris.

sections.title: A giant with a close companion
sections.text: The bright giant has a fainter stellar partner on a roughly 44-year orbit. A more distant spectroscopic binary adds another pair to the wider family.

sections.title: A pointer with a different origin
sections.text: Dubhe is not a member of the Ursa Major moving group shared by five of the Dipper’s central stars. The familiar pattern combines a real stellar association with unrelated foreground or background landmarks.

msc-12415-4858.name: Gamma Centauri
msc-12415-4858.introduction: is a bright southern binary in Centaurus. Two similar white stars blend into a single naked-eye point.

sections.title: Two stars on a human timescale
sections.text: The main pair takes roughly 85 years to orbit. Their changing positions can be followed across generations of observations, allowing their combined gravitational mass to be measured.

sections.title: A possible much wider family
sections.text: Tau Centauri shares its motion and may be gravitationally bound at a separation exceeding a light-year. That wider association is less compact than the well-established inner binary.

bright-kochab.name: Kochab
bright-kochab.introduction: is the orange giant in the bowl of the Little Dipper. With nearby Pherkad it is traditionally known as one of the “Guardians of the Pole.”

sections.title: An earlier guide to north
sections.text: Earth’s slowly precessing axis once placed the north celestial pole closer to Kochab and Pherkad than it is today. Neither approached the pole as closely as Polaris does now.

sections.title: A giant whose interior is still debated
sections.text: Kochab has expanded to many times the Sun’s size. Its exact evolutionary state is less certain: models can place it either before or during core helium burning.

bright-markab.name: Markab
bright-markab.introduction: is a blue-white star at a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. Its traditional name refers to the mount or saddle of the flying horse.

sections.title: A star changing its fuel supply
sections.text: Its spectrum places it near the transition away from the main sequence. As central hydrogen becomes depleted, the star’s structure changes and its outer layers begin to expand.

sections.title: A square drawn in depth
sections.text: The Great Square is an apparent pattern, not a bound group. Markab, Scheat, Algenib and Alpheratz lie at different distances and have quite different physical properties.

bright-elnath.name: Elnath
bright-elnath.introduction: is the blue-white star at the tip of Taurus’s northern horn. Its position beside Auriga once earned it a designation in both constellations.

sections.title: Heavy elements in the spectrum
sections.text: Elnath has unusual surface abundances, with some heavy elements enhanced and others depleted. Such patterns show that a stellar atmosphere can sort elements rather than simply preserve a uniform mixture.

sections.title: A boundary landmark
sections.text: The star is now assigned to Taurus. Its earlier connection with Auriga reflects the history of constellation boundaries, which divide directions in the sky rather than physical regions of space.

orb6-01377-5714-a-b.name: Achernar
orb6-01377-5714-a-b.introduction: is the blue-white star at the southern end of Eridanus, the River. It is a binary whose luminous primary rotates exceptionally fast.

sections.title: A star visibly flattened by rotation
sections.text: Interferometry revealed a strongly bulging equator. Rotation also creates hotter poles and a cooler equatorial belt, making Achernar a classic test of models that go beyond spherical stars.

source.title: ESO: Interferometry reveals Achernar’s flattened shape

sections.title: Gas around a spinning star
sections.text: Achernar is a Be star, periodically surrounded by an equatorial disk of expelled gas. A fainter stellar companion follows a much wider orbit around the rapidly rotating primary.

bright-kaus-australis.name: Kaus Australis
bright-kaus-australis.introduction: is the brightest star in Sagittarius and a lower corner of the Teapot asterism. A hot primary dominates this binary’s light.

sections.title: A cooler companion in the glare
sections.text: High-resolution observations reveal a much fainter companion. Separating it from the bright primary requires more than simply pointing a small telescope at the naked-eye star.

sections.title: The southern bow
sections.text: Its name means the southern part of the bow. Together with Kaus Media and Kaus Borealis, it traces the weapon of the celestial archer, an older figure within the modern Teapot pattern.

bright-kraz.name: Kraz
bright-kraz.introduction: is the yellowish bright giant at one corner of Corvus’s four-star figure. Despite its beta designation, it is slightly fainter than Gienah, the constellation’s gamma star.

sections.title: Youth and old age are relative
sections.text: Kraz is only a few hundred million years old, yet has already evolved into a giant. More massive stars spend their fuel much faster than the Sun, reaching late life at much younger ages.

sections.title: A crow beside the cup
sections.text: Corvus, neighboring Crater and the long body of Hydra preserve an interconnected sky story. Kraz helps draw the compact crow-shaped figure above Hydra’s back.

bright-gienah.name: Gienah
bright-gienah.introduction: is the brightest star in Corvus, the Crow. A hot blue-white primary and a much fainter companion make up the system.

sections.title: An atmosphere rich in heavy elements
sections.text: The primary is a mercury-manganese star. Its unusual spectrum reflects selective accumulation and settling of elements in the atmosphere, producing a chemical pattern very different from the Sun’s.

sections.title: Two wings with similar names
sections.text: Gienah refers to a wing. A similar traditional name was also used for Epsilon Cygni, now officially Aljanah; the two are unrelated stars in different bird constellations.

bright-eltanin.name: Eltanin
bright-eltanin.introduction: is the orange giant in the head of Draco. Its name refers to the dragon, and it is the brightest star in that sprawling northern constellation.

sections.title: A failed distance measurement, a major discovery
sections.text: While trying to measure Eltanin’s parallax, James Bradley discovered stellar aberration in 1728. Earth’s motion changes the apparent direction of incoming starlight, providing evidence of its orbit around the Sun.

sections.title: The zenith star
sections.text: Eltanin passes almost overhead at Greenwich. That favorable position made it especially useful for precision observations, giving this otherwise ordinary-looking giant an outsized place in astronomical history.

orb6-05597+3713-a-b.name: Mahasim
orb6-05597+3713-a-b.introduction: is the bright component of a binary in Auriga, with a fainter main-sequence companion visible nearby through a telescope.

sections.title: A magnetic chemical map
sections.text: The primary has a strong magnetic field and an atmosphere with uneven elemental abundances. As it rotates, these chemical regions change the spectrum and brightness seen from Earth.

sections.title: A few days per turn
sections.text: Its approximately 3.6-day variation is tied to rotation. Mapping the changing spectral lines lets astronomers reconstruct surface structure on a star that looks like a point in ordinary images.

bright-beta-gruis.name: Beta Gruis
bright-beta-gruis.introduction: is the red giant also named Tiaki, in the southern constellation Grus. Its warm-looking color contrasts with blue-white Alnair nearby.

sections.title: A vast, cool envelope
sections.text: Tiaki is an asymptotic-giant-branch star, with an extended atmosphere far larger than the Sun’s. It is in a late evolutionary phase, after its long main-sequence lifetime.

sections.title: A changing red light
sections.text: Its brightness varies semi-regularly, with intervals of more orderly pulsation mixed with slower irregular changes. The star’s visible light therefore gives a changing view of a dynamic, expanded atmosphere.

bright-peacock.name: Peacock
bright-peacock.introduction: is the blue-white light at the head of Pavo, the Peacock. The bright point is a spectroscopic binary.

sections.title: A close partner
sections.text: The system’s stars orbit in about 11.8 days. Doppler shifts reveal the pairing, but the faint companion remains much less well characterized than the luminous primary.

sections.title: A modern English star name
sections.text: “Peacock” was introduced for use in a twentieth-century navigation almanac. Unlike many familiar bright-star names, it is a direct English reference to the constellation’s bird.

bright-alphard.name: Alphard
bright-alphard.introduction: is the orange giant in Hydra whose Arabic name means “the solitary one.” It stands out in an unusually sparse stretch of bright-star sky.

sections.title: A giant with a complex voice
sections.text: Small changes in its radial velocity and spectral-line shapes reveal multiple oscillations. These help distinguish motion within the star’s atmosphere from the simple wobble of an orbiting companion.

sections.title: An isolated-looking landmark
sections.text: Its lonely appearance comes from our viewpoint, not an absence of other stars in space. It marks the heart of Hydra, the longest of the modern constellations.

bright-zubeneschamali.name: Zubeneschamali
bright-zubeneschamali.introduction: is the brightest star in Libra, a hot star whose name preserves its older identity as the scorpion’s northern claw.

sections.title: The famous “green” star
sections.text: Some historical observers described it as green, although its physical spectrum is that of a blue-white B-type star. The reports illustrate how visual perception and observing conditions complicate stellar color descriptions.

sections.title: Claws became scales
sections.text: The stars now making Libra were associated with Scorpius in older traditions. Their surviving names record the change from the scorpion’s claws to the separate constellation of the Scales.

bright-scheat.name: Scheat
bright-scheat.introduction: is the red star at an upper corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. It is an evolved giant with a much cooler surface than the Square’s blue-white stars.

sections.title: A breathing corner of the square
sections.text: Scheat varies semi-regularly as its extended outer layers change. Its light does not follow the perfectly repeatable pattern of a simple eclipsing binary.

sections.title: Matter leaving the star
sections.text: Observations indicate mass loss and circumstellar material. Stars in this expanded phase help recycle gas and dust, carrying material from stellar interiors back into the surroundings.

bright-mirach.name: Mirach
bright-mirach.introduction: is a red giant in Andromeda, widely used as a stepping stone to the Andromeda Galaxy. It marks part of the princess’s body.

sections.title: A star beside a “ghost”
sections.text: The small galaxy NGC 404 lies close to Mirach in the sky and is nicknamed Mirach’s Ghost. It is vastly farther away; the apparent pairing is a chance line of sight.

sections.title: A late phase of stellar life
sections.text: Mirach’s cool surface belongs to an enormously expanded envelope. It is on the asymptotic giant branch, a late stage during which stars can lose substantial material to their surroundings.

msc-18553-2618.name: Nunki
msc-18553-2618.introduction: is the blue-white star in the handle of Sagittarius’s Teapot. Its ancient name is among the bright-star names with roots in Mesopotamian astronomy.

sections.title: Two stars hidden in the light
sections.text: Interferometry resolves two similarly bright stars in a 134.779-day orbit. Published evolutionary models estimate masses of about 6.5 and 6.3 Suns and radii of about 4.1 and 3.9 Suns. These are individual model estimates; the mass inferred dynamically from the orbit applies to the pair together.

sections.title: An orbit tilted away from us
sections.text: The orbit is inclined by only about 20 degrees to the sky plane, so eclipses are not expected. Both stars rotate rapidly: broad spectral lines can hide a close pair even when it is resolved by interferometry.

source.title: Waisberg & Katz 2026: the resolved orbit of Nunki

bright-schedar.name: Schedar
bright-schedar.introduction: is the orange giant anchoring one side of Cassiopeia’s W. Its traditional name refers to the breast of the imagined queen.

sections.title: An expanded, cooler surface
sections.text: Schedar’s orange color distinguishes it from the hotter stars nearby in the W. Its great surface area makes it luminous despite a lower temperature than the Sun.

sections.title: A familiar pattern, unrelated stars
sections.text: Cassiopeia’s five principal stars occupy different distances and evolutionary stages. Their W is a useful landmark drawn by perspective, rather than a single cluster traveling through space.

msc-14450+2704.name: Izar
msc-14450+2704.introduction: is a contrasting pair in Boötes: an orange giant and a hotter white main-sequence star about 180 AU apart in projection. A much fainter candidate brown dwarf lies roughly 4,900 AU away.

sections.title: The “loveliest” pair
sections.text: Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve called it Pulcherrima, Latin for “loveliest,” in reference to its color contrast. The perceived bluish or greenish tint of the fainter star is strengthened by the orange primary beside it.

sections.title: Why A, B and D?
sections.text: The catalog retains the Multiple Star Catalog labels A, B and D. D identifies Gaia DR3 1279752168030730496, a candidate brown dwarf found through its similar proper motion and parallax. Its membership and substellar nature remain provisional; the missing letter is not evidence for a missing confirmed star.

source.title: Kervella et al. (2022), section 5.1.5

sections.title: A shared distance, with limits
sections.text: The map uses an approximate common distance of 62 parsecs (about 203 light-years), based on Hipparcos. Gaia’s bright-primary solution is affected by saturation, and B has no Gaia DR3 parallax. Their uncertain individual parallaxes cannot resolve the true depth within the system. The displayed separations preserve their measured sky directions; they are projected separations, not a measured three-dimensional orbit.

source.title: Hipparcos, HIP 72105; approximate shared system distance

sections.title: Another possible companion
sections.text: Kervella and colleagues also identify 2MASS J14454000+2615167 as a common-proper-motion candidate about 186,000 AU away in projection, nearly three light-years. That much wider candidate is distinct from MSC component D. Its physical association remains uncertain, so it is described here without assigning a new component letter or a bound orbit.

source.title: Kervella et al. (2022), section 5.1.5

bright-menkar.name: Menkar
bright-menkar.introduction: is the red giant marking the head or nose of Cetus. Despite its alpha designation, it is fainter than the constellation’s Beta Ceti, Diphda.

sections.title: An atmosphere large enough to measure
sections.text: Interferometry resolves Menkar’s apparent diameter and tests models of its cool atmosphere. Molecular absorption and the brightness change toward the apparent edge help reveal conditions in its outer layers.

sections.title: An enormous, cool star
sections.text: Its radius is roughly a hundred times the Sun’s. The huge surface makes Menkar luminous even though its photosphere is cool enough for molecules to survive.

msc-13252-1110.name: Spica
msc-13252-1110.introduction: is the blue-white beacon in Virgo. Its brilliant point is dominated by a close pair of hot stars, with a further companion detected by interferometry.

sections.title: Stars stretched by tides
sections.text: The pair circles in about four days. Their mutual gravity distorts their shapes, producing slight brightness changes as different areas turn toward us, rather than ordinary eclipses.

sections.title: Separating the stars
sections.text: The close pair has published individual masses of about 11.4 and 7.2 Suns. An interferometric study also detected a third source. Its light must be treated separately when interpreting combined observations; brightness measured for the whole system does not belong to either close-binary star.

source.title: Frost et al.: interferometric B-star multiplicity
Tkachenko et al. 2016: resolved Spica binary parameters

bright-bellatrix.name: Bellatrix
bright-bellatrix.introduction: is the blue-white star on Orion’s shoulder, opposite the red Betelgeuse. Its name is commonly translated as “female warrior.”

sections.title: Hotter than its color suggests
sections.text: Bellatrix radiates strongly in the ultraviolet. The light visible to our eyes represents only part of the energy emitted by its hot surface.

sections.title: An unsettled evolutionary label
sections.text: Its spectrum has a giant classification, but models suggest it may still be burning hydrogen in its core. High-resolution observations have also challenged the idea that two similarly bright stars explain its properties.

bright-mimosa.name: Mimosa
bright-mimosa.introduction: is Beta Crucis, the blue-white star on one arm of the Southern Cross. It is a multiple system dominated by a hot, massive primary.

sections.title: Pulsations reveal the interior
sections.text: The primary is a Beta Cephei variable with oscillations lasting a few hours. Combining its brightness changes with polarization measurements allows unusually detailed tests of its internal structure and orientation.

source.title: Cotton et al. 2021: Polarimetric detection of oscillation modes in Beta Crucis

sections.title: More than one companion
sections.text: A spectroscopic companion follows a roughly five-year orbit, while a faint young star lies farther out. Their light and activity must be separated when interpreting the bright primary’s measurements.

bright-phact.name: Phact
bright-phact.introduction: is the brightest star in Columba, the Dove, south of Orion. It is a hot, rapidly rotating blue-white star.

sections.title: A disk written into the spectrum
sections.text: Phact is a Be star: emission lines reveal gas around it. The circumstellar material is associated with a rapidly rotating star, rather than a dusty planet-forming disk around a newborn Sun-like star.

sections.title: A dove below the hunter
sections.text: Columba was introduced to European star maps much later than Orion. Its compact figure occupies a patch of southern sky beneath the far more conspicuous hunter and his dogs.

msc-17373-4300.name: Sargas
msc-17373-4300.introduction: is the yellow-white star near the bend of Scorpius’s tail. It is a binary dominated by a luminous, evolved primary.

sections.title: A giant flattened by rotation
sections.text: Interferometry shows an equatorial bulge and a temperature difference between the poles and equator. Such rapid rotation is unusual for an expanded star and has prompted models involving a past stellar merger.

sections.title: A partner in the glare
sections.text: A close, fainter companion is detected beside the bright star. Its presence adds another part to the system’s history without proving the proposed merger scenario for the primary.

bright-eta-centauri.name: Eta Centauri
bright-eta-centauri.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Centaurus. It belongs to the broad Scorpius–Centaurus association of young stars sharing a common origin.

sections.title: A day shorter than Earth’s
sections.text: Its rapid rotation carries the surface around in less than a day. Broad absorption lines are one clue to that speed.

sections.title: A variable gas disk
sections.text: Eta Centauri is a Be star, with emission from material around it. Changes in the circumstellar gas contribute to its variability, allowing astronomers to follow exchanges of matter between a hot star and its surroundings.

bright-canopus.name: Canopus
bright-canopus.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Earth’s night sky, a brilliant white beacon in Carina. It is far more distant and intrinsically luminous than Sirius.

sections.title: A star beyond the red-giant stage
sections.text: Canopus is interpreted as a core-helium-burning star on a blue loop: it has already expanded and cooled, then moved back toward higher surface temperatures. Stellar evolution need not follow a one-way change from blue to red.

sections.title: A guide for spacecraft
sections.text: Its brightness and position away from the Sun’s usual path made Canopus useful for spacecraft attitude sensors. It became a navigation landmark far beyond its traditional role for sailors.

msc-12372-6908.name: Alpha Muscae
msc-12372-6908.introduction: is the brightest star in Musca, the small constellation of the Fly beside the Southern Cross. A hot B-type primary dominates its light.

sections.title: A young stellar neighborhood
sections.text: It belongs to the Lower Centaurus–Crux subgroup of the Scorpius–Centaurus association. The group provides a shared age and birthplace context for stars now spread over a large area of sky.

sections.title: Tiny changes in a bright star
sections.text: Small brightness variations are associated with stellar pulsations. Their timescales probe the behavior of a massive star, rather than indicating that the point of light is physically blinking on and off.

msc-12266-6306.name: Acrux
msc-12266-6306.introduction: is the brilliant light at the foot of the Southern Cross. A telescope begins to separate what the eye blends into one of the sky’s brightest stars.

sections.title: A family inside the double
sections.text: The two principal visual components are hot B-type stars, and the brighter one is itself a close spectroscopic binary. Additional companions make the wider system still more intricate.

sections.title: Finding south from the Cross
sections.text: The long axis from Gacrux through Acrux points toward the south celestial pole. The Cross is an orientation guide, though Acrux itself is not a southern pole star.

bright-leepwal.name: Leepwal
bright-leepwal.introduction: is Zeta Centauri, a hot blue-white binary in the body of the Centaur. Its primary is much more massive than the Sun.

sections.title: An eight-day partnership
sections.text: Spectral lines reveal two stars in an eccentric orbit lasting just over eight days. Their separation is far too small for the unaided eye to distinguish.

sections.title: A Marshallese name
sections.text: Leepwal comes from the Marshall Islands’ sky traditions and was approved internationally in 2024. It joins a growing set of bright-star names that reflect cultures beyond the familiar Arabic and Greek traditions.

msc-14585-4308.name: Beta Lupi
msc-14585-4308.introduction: is a blue-white giant in Lupus, the Wolf. It belongs to the young Upper Centaurus–Lupus stellar association.

sections.title: A massive star’s pulse
sections.text: Beta Lupi is a Beta Cephei variable with a principal cycle of about 5.6 hours. These small oscillations let astronomers study the interiors of massive stars.

sections.title: Young, yet already changing
sections.text: Although only tens of millions of years old, it is approaching the end of its core-hydrogen-burning phase. Its rapid evolution contrasts with the Sun’s much longer main-sequence lifetime.

bright-atria.name: Atria
bright-atria.introduction: is the orange beacon at the brightest corner of Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle. Its name contracts its designation, Alpha Trianguli Australis.

sections.title: A giant on a grand scale
sections.text: Atria is an evolved, luminous star with an enormous cool envelope. Its orange color indicates surface temperature; the large emitting area accounts for its strong luminosity.

sections.title: A triangle of perspective
sections.text: The Southern Triangle is easy to recognize, but its three main stars are not a compact stellar family. Their apparent arrangement serves as a sky landmark for southern observers.

msc-14038-6022.name: Hadar
msc-14038-6022.introduction: is the bright blue-white system beside Alpha Centauri. Together they form the southern “Pointers,” but Hadar lies far beyond its nearby-looking neighbor.

sections.title: A triple behind the bright point
sections.text: The inner pair consists of two massive stars in a strongly eccentric orbit of almost a year. A third B-type star lies farther out.

sections.title: Asteroseismology in a multiple system
sections.text: The bright components show pulsations that help probe their interiors. Combining these oscillations with orbital measurements provides complementary information about stellar structure and mass.

msc-02039+4220.name: Almach
msc-02039+4220.introduction: is a multiple system in Andromeda celebrated for its telescope view: a bright golden star beside a fainter blue-white point.

sections.title: A colorful double with hidden layers
sections.text: The bright component is an evolved giant. The apparently single blue-white companion is itself a close multiple, so resolving the attractive visual pair is only the first step into the system.

sections.title: Color shaped by contrast
sections.text: The large temperature difference between the visible components makes the pair especially striking. Their apparent colors are also influenced by comparison with one another through the eyepiece.

msc-16054-1948.name: Beta Scorpii
msc-16054-1948.introduction: is the multiple system also called Acrab, near the head of Scorpius. The catalog’s Beta Scorpii A belongs to this wider stellar family.

sections.title: Pairs within pairs
sections.text: A telescope separates the main visual components, but spectroscopy and higher-resolution observations reveal additional close companions. The familiar bright point is a hierarchy of orbits, not a simple two-star pair.

sections.title: A shared young origin
sections.text: The system belongs to Upper Scorpius, a nearby association of young stars. Its hot components have evolved together over only millions of years, providing a useful comparison with much older nearby Sun-like systems.

adhara.name: Adhara
adhara.introduction: is the blue-white binary in Canis Major, south of Sirius. A luminous hot primary dominates its light and makes it one of the brightest stars in the night sky.

sections.title: Brilliance beyond visible light
sections.text: Adhara is an exceptionally strong source of extreme-ultraviolet radiation. Its importance at those wavelengths is much greater than its visible-light ranking alone suggests.

sections.title: A difficult visual companion
sections.text: A much fainter companion lies close beside the primary in the sky. The enormous brightness contrast makes separating them through a telescope challenging, despite their wider spacing than many spectroscopic binaries.

bright-kaus-media.name: Kaus Media
bright-kaus-media.introduction: is the orange giant in the bow of Sagittarius, also part of the Teapot figure. Its name means the middle part of the bow.

sections.title: An archer inside a teapot
sections.text: Kaus Australis, Kaus Media and Kaus Borealis mark successive parts of the archer’s bow. The Teapot is a newer observing pattern made from some of the same stars.

sections.title: A cooler surface, a larger star
sections.text: Kaus Media has evolved beyond the main sequence and expanded into a giant. Its warm color contrasts with the hotter blue-white stars nearby, even though they appear together in the same figure.

bright-epsilon-centauri.name: Epsilon Centauri
bright-epsilon-centauri.introduction: is a hot blue-white giant in Centaurus. It belongs to the Lower Centaurus–Crux subgroup of the Scorpius–Centaurus association.

sections.title: Multiple pulses in the light
sections.text: It is a Beta Cephei variable with more than one oscillation period. These small variations arise within the star and can be used to test models of massive stellar interiors.

sections.title: A young star with a fast life
sections.text: Its age is measured in tens of millions of years, yet it already shows an evolved spectrum. A massive star can race through stages that a Sun-like star takes billions of years to reach.

msc-02318+8916.name: Polaris
msc-02318+8916.introduction: is the North Star, near the direction of Earth’s rotation axis. Its bright yellow supergiant belongs to a triple system, with one close companion and another much farther out.

sections.title: A distance-scale heartbeat
sections.text: Polaris is a Cepheid, gently changing size and brightness over about four days. Cepheid pulsation periods are linked to luminosity, making this nearby example important for understanding how astronomers measure cosmic distances.

sections.title: Spots on the North Star
sections.text: CHARA observations published in 2024 resolved bright and dark surface regions and followed the close companion’s orbit. The orbital motion provides a direct check on the mass of the pulsating primary.

source.title: CHARA: Polaris’s orbit, mass and spotted surface, 2024

bright-zeta-ophiuchi.name: Zeta Ophiuchi
bright-zeta-ophiuchi.introduction: is a hot, rapidly rotating runaway star in Ophiuchus. It is moving unusually fast relative to nearby interstellar material.

sections.title: A bow wave in space
sections.text: Its stellar wind collides with gas and dust ahead of its path, forming an arcing bow shock visible in infrared images. The surrounding structure makes the star’s motion tangible.

source.title: Green et al. 2022: Three-dimensional models of Zeta Ophiuchi’s bow shock

sections.title: An uncertain ejection story
sections.text: A supernova in a former binary or encounters among several stars can eject a massive star. Reconstructing Zeta Ophiuchi’s specific origin remains an active problem; the bow shock alone does not identify the event that launched it.

bright-hassaleh.name: Hassaleh
bright-hassaleh.introduction: is the orange giant Iota Aurigae, marking part of the Charioteer’s figure. Interstellar dust dims and reddens its light on the way to Earth.

sections.title: A cool star with hot plasma
sections.text: Although its visible surface is cool, X-rays reveal much hotter gas in the outer atmosphere. Magnetic structures can heat a small amount of material far above the photospheric temperature.

sections.title: A name with a missing history
sections.text: Hassaleh appeared in a twentieth-century star atlas, but its linguistic origin is uncertain. The older name Al Kab referred to the ankle of the rein-holder.

bright-alpha-lupi.name: Alpha Lupi
bright-alpha-lupi.introduction: is the brightest star in Lupus, the Wolf. It is a hot blue-white giant in the young Upper Centaurus–Lupus association.

sections.title: A short stellar heartbeat
sections.text: Alpha Lupi is a Beta Cephei variable, with small brightness changes over a few hours. The pulsations provide information about a massive star’s interior without requiring its surface to be resolved.

sections.title: Part of a dispersed nursery
sections.text: Its association is a loose family rather than a compact cluster. Shared motion and youth connect stars that now occupy a large region around Centaurus and Lupus.

bright-kappa-scorpii.name: Kappa Scorpii
bright-kappa-scorpii.introduction: is a close binary in the curved tail of Scorpius. The bright component is a hot, massive star whose light changes subtly.

sections.title: An orbit and a pulse
sections.text: The stars orbit in roughly 196 days, while the primary pulsates on a much shorter timescale of about 4.8 hours. Spectroscopy helps distinguish those two kinds of motion.

sections.title: A view inside a massive star
sections.text: Its Beta Cephei oscillations let astronomers test how material mixes and energy moves within hot stars. The companion supplies additional orbital information that a truly isolated pulsator would not offer.

orb6-16003-2237-a-b.name: Dschubba
orb6-16003-2237-a-b.introduction: is a blue-white binary marking the forehead of Scorpius. Its bright primary is surrounded at times by a disk of gas.

sections.title: A star that grew visibly brighter
sections.text: Around 2000, Dschubba brightened markedly as circumstellar emission developed. Changes in its gas disk can alter the appearance of a star long treated as a relatively steady constellation landmark.

sections.title: Close approaches in an elongated orbit
sections.text: The companion returns on a highly eccentric orbit of about 10.5 years. Monitoring the pair near closest approach helps investigate the relationship between binary interaction and the primary’s disk.

bright-mirzam.name: Mirzam
bright-mirzam.introduction: is the hot blue-white star west of Sirius in Canis Major. Its name refers to an announcer or herald, fitting its rising ahead of the Dog Star.

sections.title: A star with several rhythms
sections.text: Mirzam is a Beta Cephei variable with multiple pulsations near six hours. Their overlapping rhythms create a more complex signal than a single regular brightening and fading.

sections.title: A laboratory for stellar interiors
sections.text: The brightness changes are too small to stand out to the eye, but precision observations reveal them clearly. They make this conspicuous constellation star useful for studying the structure of massive stars.

bright-betelgeuse.name: Betelgeuse
bright-betelgeuse.introduction: is the red supergiant on Orion’s shoulder. Its enormous, changing atmosphere makes it one of the few stars beyond the Sun whose surface can be studied in detail.

sections.title: The Great Dimming
sections.text: In 2019–2020 it faded dramatically. Observations linked the event to surface cooling and newly formed dust obscuring part of the star. It was not evidence that a supernova had already begun.

source.title: ESO: The dust responsible for Betelgeuse’s Great Dimming

sections.title: A likely hidden companion
sections.text: VLT images reported in July 2026 strengthened the case for a faint stellar companion, Betelgeuse B. Its possible influence on the supergiant’s evolution is being investigated; the star’s eventual supernova date remains uncertain.

source.title: ESO: Strongest evidence yet for Betelgeuse’s companion, July 2026

bright-mirfak.name: Mirfak
bright-mirfak.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant at the center of the Alpha Persei star cluster. It is the brightest star in Perseus, outshining the more famous variable Algol.

sections.title: A cluster for binoculars
sections.text: A wide view reveals young stars scattered around Mirfak. This is a real stellar group, rather than just a chance constellation pattern, and its common origin gives astronomers an age reference.

sections.title: The most conspicuous elder
sections.text: Mirfak has already evolved into a supergiant while many cluster members remain on the main sequence. The contrast shows how a star’s initial mass changes the pace of evolution even within one coeval family.

bright-suhail.name: Suhail
bright-suhail.introduction: is the orange supergiant Lambda Velorum in Vela. Its large, cool envelope gives it a very different appearance from nearby blue-white stars.

sections.title: A slowly changing giant
sections.text: Suhail is a slow irregular variable. Its changing light reflects activity in a vast, extended atmosphere rather than the clockwork eclipse of a close binary.

sections.title: A name shared across southern skies
sections.text: Versions of Suhail were historically applied to several bright southern stars. The modern name identifies Lambda Velorum specifically, helping distinguish it from Canopus and the Gamma Velorum system.

msc-00567+6043.name: Gamma Cassiopeiae
msc-00567+6043.introduction: is the hot star at the center of Cassiopeia’s W. It is a binary and the prototype of a class of variable Be stars.

sections.title: A star feeding a disk
sections.text: Rapid rotation and episodes of mass ejection produce a disk of gas around the primary. Changes in that material have caused large historical variations in the star’s brightness.

sections.title: An X-ray puzzle
sections.text: Its unusually strong, hot X-ray emission has inspired competing explanations involving the star, its disk and its companion. The origin of the high-energy activity is not settled simply by identifying the binary.

spectroscopic-bright-antares.name: Antares
spectroscopic-bright-antares.introduction: is the red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius, accompanied by a much hotter, fainter blue star. Its name evokes a rival to the reddish planet Mars.

sections.title: A moving atmosphere mapped directly
sections.text: Interferometry has resolved the supergiant’s surface and mapped gas motions above it. Unexpected turbulence in the extended atmosphere helps frame the puzzle of how red supergiants lose so much material.

source.title: ESO: Resolving Antares’s surface and atmospheric motions

sections.title: A striking unequal pair
sections.text: The blue companion can look greenish beside the overwhelming red primary through a telescope. That apparent tint is influenced by visual contrast; it does not mean the companion emits predominantly green light.

msc-17336-3706.name: Shaula
msc-17336-3706.introduction: is the brighter of the two stars marking Scorpius’s sting. What looks like one blue-white star is a triple system.

sections.title: A close pair and a third star
sections.text: The inner companion circles in about six days, while another hot star orbits the pair in roughly three years. The short-period companion is interpreted as a young star still approaching the main sequence.

sections.title: Two kinds of changing light
sections.text: The system includes eclipses and small pulsations of the luminous primary. Distinguishing the orbital effects from the star’s own oscillations helps recover the properties of the individual members.

bright-markeb.name: Markeb
bright-markeb.introduction: is the blue-white binary Kappa Velorum, one of the four stars of the False Cross. That asterism is often mistaken for the nearby Southern Cross.

sections.title: A close binary in the sails
sections.text: Spectroscopy reveals two stars orbiting in about 117 days. Their combined light makes a single naked-eye landmark in Vela.

sections.title: A probe of intervening clouds
sections.text: Narrow absorption lines reveal interstellar gas between Markeb and Earth. Changes in those lines over time expose small-scale cloud structure as the line of sight moves across the material.

bright-lesath.name: Lesath
bright-lesath.introduction: is the hot blue-white star beside Shaula at the tip of Scorpius’s tail. The two draw the scorpion’s sting and are sometimes called the Cat’s Eyes.

sections.title: A pair in the drawing
sections.text: Lesath and Shaula form a conspicuous optical pair. Shaula’s known close companions belong to its own system; being beside it in the sky does not make Lesath one of those components.

sections.title: Most of the energy is unseen
sections.text: Lesath’s high surface temperature shifts much of its radiation into the ultraviolet. Its visible brightness therefore understates its total energy output compared with a cooler star of the same visual magnitude.

spectroscopic-bright-avior.name: Avior
spectroscopic-bright-avior.introduction: is a southern binary whose light combines an orange giant and a hot blue star. It marks a corner of the False Cross.

sections.title: Very different stars, one point
sections.text: The cooler giant and hotter companion contribute different parts of the blended spectrum. Their contrast makes Avior useful for studying the difficulties of separating stellar properties in unresolved systems.

sections.title: A name made for navigation
sections.text: Avior was coined for a twentieth-century navigation almanac. Along with Peacock, it is an example of a modern name introduced to give navigators a convenient label for a prominent southern star.

msc-12084-5043.name: Delta Centauri
msc-12084-5043.introduction: is a hot Be star in Centaurus, associated with the young Lower Centaurus–Crux population. Its bright primary is part of a wider multiple system.

sections.title: Gas around a rapid rotator
sections.text: Emission lines reveal circumstellar gas, while broad absorption lines show rapid rotation. The disk and star together produce a more complicated spectrum than an unobscured spherical stellar surface.

sections.title: Companions at different scales
sections.text: High-resolution observations reveal a close companion, with additional nearby stars sharing the system’s motion. Their wider relationships are less simple than the appearance of one bright catalog point suggests.

bright-saiph.name: Saiph
bright-saiph.introduction: is the blue supergiant at one of Orion’s feet, opposite Rigel. It is a hot, massive star whose bright appearance comes from far beyond the nearby stellar neighborhood.

sections.title: A great deal of invisible light
sections.text: Its high temperature sends much of its energy into the ultraviolet. Comparing Saiph and Rigel by visible brightness alone therefore does not compare their total energy outputs.

sections.title: A brief supergiant phase
sections.text: Saiph has already evolved away from ordinary main-sequence life. Massive stars pass through these enlarged, unstable stages quickly, returning matter to space through stellar winds before their final fate.

bright-enif.name: Enif
bright-enif.introduction: is the orange supergiant marking the nose of Pegasus. Although outside the Great Square, it is usually the constellation’s brightest star.

sections.title: An unusually changeable beacon
sections.text: Enif is a slow irregular variable, with rare reports of much more dramatic brightening. These unusual events have prompted discussion of powerful flares or disturbances in supergiant atmospheres.

sections.title: A huge, cool envelope
sections.text: Its surface is cooler than the Sun’s, but the star is vastly larger. The combination produces an intensely luminous star with a warm color, illustrating why temperature alone cannot predict brightness.

msc-05320-0018.name: Mintaka
msc-05320-0018.introduction: is the westernmost star of Orion’s Belt. It is a multiple system dominated by a close pair of hot, massive stars.

sections.title: A clockwork eclipse in the Belt
sections.text: The principal pair orbits in about 5.7 days and undergoes shallow eclipses. Modeling the changing light together with orbital velocities helps estimate the stars’ individual sizes and masses.

sections.title: A hierarchy beyond the eclipse
sections.text: Other companions orbit at larger separations, and a more distant visible component is itself a binary. The single Belt star is therefore a family with several levels of orbital structure.

msc-05407-0157.name: Alnitak
msc-05407-0157.introduction: is the easternmost star of Orion’s Belt. Its multiple system is dominated by a very hot O-type supergiant.

sections.title: A rare bright O star
sections.text: O stars are exceptionally hot and short-lived. Alnitak’s strong ultraviolet radiation and stellar wind make its environment very different from the quiet surroundings of a Sun-like star.

sections.title: Companions and neighboring clouds
sections.text: A close companion accompanies the supergiant, with another star farther out. The famous Flame and Horsehead nebulae lie nearby in the sky, making this part of Orion especially rich in dust, gas and young stars.

bright-aspidiske.name: Aspidiske
bright-aspidiske.introduction: is the white supergiant Iota Carinae, a corner of the False Cross. Its name refers to a small shield.

sections.title: A misleading cross
sections.text: Aspidiske, Avior, Markeb and Alsephina form the False Cross across Carina and Vela. Confusing it with Crux gives a misleading guide to the south celestial pole.

sections.title: Crossing toward cooler temperatures
sections.text: Aspidiske is an expanded A-type supergiant crossing the relatively sparsely populated gap between hot main-sequence stars and cool giants. This short evolutionary passage helps explain why stars with its properties are uncommon.

rigel.name: Rigel
rigel.introduction: is the blue supergiant at Orion’s foot, the brilliant primary of a multiple system. Much fainter hot companions accompany the star that dominates our view.

sections.title: A triple beside the supergiant
sections.text: Rigel B contains the close pair Ba and Bb, with C farther out. Together with the supergiant, they make a hierarchical four-star family whose components share one system story despite their very different brightnesses.

sections.title: A changing blue supergiant
sections.text: Rigel shows small pulsations and loses material through a stellar wind. Its changing light and spectrum let astronomers study the interior and atmosphere of a massive star in an advanced evolutionary phase.

bright-naos.name: Naos
bright-naos.introduction: is the extremely hot O-type supergiant Zeta Puppis. Its name refers to the ship, recalling the old constellation Argo Navis.

sections.title: A powerful stellar wind
sections.text: Naos pours much of its radiation into the ultraviolet and drives a fast, dense outflow. Features moving through its wind reveal structure rather than a perfectly smooth stream of escaping gas.

sections.title: A massive runaway
sections.text: Its motion identifies it as a runaway star. Proposed histories include binary interaction, a stellar merger or dynamical ejection; reconstructing the specific sequence is harder than establishing that it is moving unusually fast.

msc-08095-4720.name: Regor
msc-08095-4720.introduction: is the bright Gamma Velorum system in Vela. Its best-known pair combines a stripped Wolf–Rayet star with a massive O-type companion.

sections.title: An exposed stellar interior
sections.text: The Wolf–Rayet star has lost much of its outer envelope, revealing material enriched by nuclear reactions. Its broad emission lines come from a dense, fast stellar wind.

sections.title: Winds crashing into winds
sections.text: The two massive stars circle in about 78.5 days. Where their winds collide, gas heats to X-ray-emitting temperatures. Other nearby components and the young Vela OB2 population place this binary in a wider stellar family.

bright-deneb.name: Deneb
bright-deneb.introduction: is the white supergiant at the tail of Cygnus and a corner of the Summer Triangle. It is vastly farther away and more luminous than fellow Triangle stars Vega and Altair.

sections.title: A distance with consequences
sections.text: Deneb’s distance remains uncertain, and that uncertainty carries directly into estimates of its luminosity and size. Its familiar brightness in our sky should not be mistaken for a precisely known physical output.

sections.title: A subtly variable supergiant
sections.text: Small brightness and spectral changes make it the prototype of Alpha Cygni variables. Pulsations and its stellar wind provide clues to an advanced stage of massive-star evolution.

bright-wezen.name: Wezen
bright-wezen.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant in Canis Major. It appears less conspicuous than nearby Sirius because it lies much farther away.

sections.title: A Sun-like temperature on a giant scale
sections.text: Its surface temperature is broadly similar to the Sun’s, but its enormous radius gives it a vastly greater emitting area. Similar color can therefore hide a profound difference in stellar size and luminosity.

sections.title: A short, massive life
sections.text: Wezen evolved rapidly because of its high mass. Its supergiant state and mass loss help astronomers investigate the late stages of stars much more massive than our own.

bright-sadr.name: Sadr
bright-sadr.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant at the crossing point of the Northern Cross. Its name refers to the breast of Cygnus, the Swan.

sections.title: A star amid glowing clouds
sections.text: Images place Sadr against the rich IC 1318 nebular region. Apparent overlap does not by itself establish which gas is physically close to the star or which source powers it.

sections.title: Near the pulsation strip
sections.text: Sadr’s spectrum and slow velocity changes place it near the realm of pulsating yellow supergiants. Its variations are more complicated than the regular cycle of a classical Cepheid.

bright-alnilam.name: Alnilam
bright-alnilam.introduction: is the middle star of Orion’s Belt, a luminous blue supergiant. Unlike the Belt’s other two principal stars, its bright appearance is usually discussed as one dominant star rather than a well-established compact multiple.

sections.title: A wind carrying matter away
sections.text: Alnilam drives a fast stellar wind that carries material away from its surface. Its relatively simple spectrum also makes it useful for studying interstellar gas through the absorption imprinted on the passing starlight.

sections.title: An apparent line across deep space
sections.text: Mintaka, Alnilam and Alnitak form a remarkably straight pattern from Earth, but their distances differ. Their similar apparent brightness conceals major differences in luminosity and system structure.

bright-aludra.name: Aludra
bright-aludra.introduction: is the blue supergiant Eta Canis Majoris, near the tail of the Great Dog. It remains conspicuous despite its great distance.

sections.title: A reference for supergiants
sections.text: Its spectrum is a standard for the B5 Ia class. Astronomers use such anchors to compare hot, very luminous stellar atmospheres and classify less familiar stars.

sections.title: A quietly changing light
sections.text: Aludra shows small variations characteristic of evolved supergiants. Its pulsations and wind reveal that even a seemingly steady constellation star can have a dynamic atmosphere and a changing energy output.

bright-arneb.name: Arneb
bright-arneb.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant in Lepus, the Hare beneath Orion. Its traditional name refers to the hare itself.

sections.title: An enormous star below Orion
sections.text: Arneb’s radius is roughly a hundred times the Sun’s. If placed at the center of our Solar System, its surface would extend beyond Mercury’s orbit.

sections.title: A late stage with an uncertain route
sections.text: Its mass and evolved spectrum place it in a short-lived phase of stellar evolution. Whether such a star is crossing toward cooler temperatures or returning from a previous red-supergiant stage requires more than color alone to determine.
